product.title: Mandarin 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twelve Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Mandarin: pīnyīn printed right above every Chinese character, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Mandarin builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a pīnyīn chart, four-tone practice, measure words, an A1 grammar summary, and 150 core characters. Mandarin grammar is kinder than its reputation: no verb conjugation, no tenses, no plurals. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up — 是 with adjectives, the “very” that isn’t, measure words, time before the verb, and 了.

cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Mandarin Chinese for complete beginners — from saying hello and haggling over prices to talking about yesterday and tomorrow.
cover_design.catatan: Pīnyīn printed above every character, a word-for-word translation under every line of dialogue.

blocks.text: Mandarin has a reputation that stops people before they start: thousands of characters, four tones, and words you supposedly can't guess. That reputation is half true. The half nobody mentions is that **Mandarin grammar is among the simplest in the world** — and that simple half is the one you use every day.

Mandarin verbs never change form. No *am / is / are*, no third-person -s, no past tense, no plurals, no grammatical gender, no endings that shift with the speaker. 我去 *wǒ qù* = I go; 他去 *tā qù* = he goes; 昨天我去 *zuótiān wǒ qù* = yesterday I went. The verb is exactly the same in all three. If you have ever wrestled with irregular verbs in French or Spanish, this is very good news.

Only two things are genuinely hard: **tones** and **characters**. This course handles both differently from most books. Tones are drilled from the very first page, not parked in an introduction and forgotten. Characters are never left bare — pīnyīn is printed **right above each character**, the way children's books in China do it, so you can read whole sentences from Unit 1 without memorizing a single character first.

The twelve units are not a random list of topics. Each one targets a spot where learners most often go wrong: 是 used in the wrong place, 很 mistaken for “very”, measure words left out, time expressions put in the wrong order, and 了 mistaken for a past tense. These are not fixed by memorizing rules but by saying sentences over and over until the wrong version starts to sound strange.

How to use it: one unit per sitting, twenty to thirty minutes. Read the dialogues out loud — out loud, not in your head. Mandarin is a language where meaning lives in the rise and fall of your voice, and you cannot train your voice with your eyes.
Enjoy the journey. 加油 — *jiāyóu*, you can do it.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones set up.

blocks.text: This course is built for self-study, with no teacher beside you. Every unit has the same layout, so after Unit 2 you no longer have to think about how to study — you just study.
Inside each unit

items: **对话 — Dialogue.** A short, natural conversation, not made-up example sentences. Each line has three layers: Chinese characters with pīnyīn above them, a readable English translation, and a **literal translation** that shows the original structure word by word.
**Notes.** Explanations of the things in the dialogue that will make you ask questions. They come after the dialogue, not before, so you ask first and get answers second.
**Grammar boxes.** One pattern, one box. Tables and examples, not jargon.
**Extra sections.** Things you need that aren't grammar: money, numbers, politeness, surviving real situations.
**Vocabulary in this unit.** Every new word in the unit, with pīnyīn and meaning.
**Exercises + answer key.** Six exercises, with the answers right below. Do them first, then check — a key you peek at too early teaches you nothing.
**Wave review.** One short task that pulls earlier units back to the surface.

blocks.text: The rules that really make the difference

items: **Read out loud.** Mandarin separates meanings by tone. A tone that only lives in your head never reaches your mouth. If you pick just one rule from this list, pick this one.
**One unit a day, not two.** What counts is not how long you sit, but how many days in a row you sit. Twenty minutes every day beats three hours once a week, and by a wide margin.

**Don't memorize characters in Unit 1.** That is what the pīnyīn above them is for. Characters will stick on their own because you see the same words again and again, not because you copy them fifty times.
**The literal translation is study material, not decoration.** It is where the way Mandarin thinks becomes visible. Read it even when it sounds odd — it is supposed to.
**Review yesterday's unit for five minutes before starting a new one.** Just cover the meaning column and say the words again. Those five minutes are what keep Unit 1 alive by Unit 12.

blocks.title: Signs used in this course
items: **[你好|nǐ hǎo]** — pīnyīn printed small, right above the character. Every Chinese character in this course is treated this way.
*literally:* — the third line under each line of dialogue, the original structure word by word.
⚠️ — the spots where learners most often go wrong. Pause for a moment whenever you see it.
**By the end of this unit you can:** — a list of real abilities, not a list of topics. If you can't do them at the end of the unit, go through it again before moving on.

front.title: Pīnyīn: reading the sounds of Mandarin

blocks.text: Pīnyīn is the official system for writing Mandarin sounds in the Latin alphabet. It is used in Chinese primary schools, on phone keyboards, and throughout this course. One thing to understand right now: **pīnyīn is not English.** The letters are borrowed; the sounds are not.

The most expensive mistake you can make in your first week is reading pīnyīn with English habits. *c* is not “k”, *q* is not “k”, *x* is not “ks”, *zh* is not “z”, and *i* doesn't always sound like “ee”. This page sorts that out once and for all.
Initial sounds (声母 shēngmǔ) that trip up English speakers

head: Pīnyīn
How it sounds
Compare
Example
rows: Like the p, t, k in *spy, sty, sky* — **no puff of air**; not a voiced English b, d, g
Same as b, d, g above but with a **strong puff of air**
**ts** with a puff, like the “ts” in *cats* followed by a breath
**ts** without a puff, like the “ds” in *kids*
Tongue **curled back**, like English j / ch / sh but deeper in the mouth
Not an English r — tongue curled, close to the “s” in *pleasure*
Tongue **flat and forward**, tip behind the lower teeth. j ≈ “jee”, q ≈ “chee” with a puff, x ≈ a thin “shee”
Rougher than English h, from the back of the throat

blocks.title: The three pairs most often mixed up
items: **j / zh** — [鸡|jī] chicken vs [知|zhī] know. j: tongue forward; zh: tongue curled.
**q / ch** — [七|qī] seven vs [吃|chī] eat. Same idea, but q sounds thinner.
**x / sh** — [西|xī] west vs [十|shí] ten. x is thin, at the teeth; sh is dark, at the back.
Check yourself: put a finger in front of your mouth. j-q-x spread your lips into a smile; zh-ch-sh push your lips slightly forward.

blocks.text: Tricky final sounds (韵母 yùnmǔ)

head: Written
Pronounced
Example
rows: **-i** after z, c, s, zh, ch, sh, r
Not “eh”, but like the “u” in *duh*, held a little longer
**ü** (written u after j, q, x, y)
Say “ee” with your lips rounded as for “oo” (like German ü)
Different meanings! -n: tongue tip on the roof of the mouth; -ng: back of the tongue

blocks.title: The most useful five-minute drill
items: Say these pairs ten times each: **sì / shí** (4 / 10), **jī / zhī**, **qù / chù**, **fàn / fàng**, **nǚ / nǔ**.
Record yourself on your phone and listen back. Your ears catch mistakes your mouth doesn't notice — it's a trick professional interpreters use.
⚠️ Don't write pīnyīn with English spelling in your notebook (“shieh shieh” for 谢谢). That habit is very hard to get rid of later.

blocks.text: In English, the rise and fall of your voice carries attitude: “now?” and “now!” are the same word with different feelings. In Mandarin, pitch is **part of the word itself**, as important as its letters. Change the tone and you change the word, not the mood.

head: Tone
Mark
Movement
Imagine
Example
rows: The “aaah” you say at the doctor's
Rises from the middle to the top
Falls sharply from top to bottom

blocks.text: 妈骂马吗？ — *Mā mà mǎ ma?* — “Is Mom scolding the horse?” Five syllables built on the same basic sound, with the meaning decided entirely by tone. This sentence isn't a textbook joke; it shows exactly what is at stake.
Where the tone mark goes

items: The tone mark always sits on a **vowel**, never on a consonant.
If there is an **a**, the mark goes on the a: *hǎo*, *xiào*.
No a, but an **o** or **e**? The mark goes there: *lóu*, *xiè*.
With **iu** or **ui**, the mark goes on the **second** letter: *liù*, *duì*.
On an **i**, the dot disappears: *nǐ*, not *nǐ̇*.

blocks.text: Tones that change by themselves (变调 biàndiào)

head: Rule
Written
Pronounced
Example
rows: Two third tones in a row
Half third tone — just dip, don't rise again
不 bù before a fourth tone
一 yī before a fourth tone

blocks.title: Training tones without a teacher
items: **Use your hand.** Move your hand with the tone as you speak: level, up, down-and-up, down. It feels silly and works remarkably well — your body remembers movements faster than your head remembers rules.
**Practice pairs, not single words.** A tone only becomes real when it has something to contrast with: *mǎi* (buy) vs *mài* (sell), *wèn* (ask) vs *wěn* (kiss).
**Learn every word with its tone from day one**, not the letters first and the tone later. A word memorized without its tone is almost always mispronounced for life.
⚠️ The neutral tone is not “no tone” — it is short and leans on the syllable before it. [妈妈|māma], [谢谢|xièxie], [朋友|péngyou]: the second syllable is light and quick.

blocks.text: This course doesn't require you to memorize characters. The pīnyīn above each one is there so you can read full sentences from day one. But if you ignore the characters entirely, you'll get stuck where everyone who learns Mandarin through pīnyīn alone gets stuck: able to speak, unable to read.
This page gives you just enough to make characters feel logical rather than like random pictures.
Three kinds of characters

head: Type
How it works
Example
rows: A simplified drawing of a thing
[人|rén] person · [山|shān] mountain · [口|kǒu] mouth · [日|rì] sun
Two pictures joined into a new meaning
[好|hǎo] good = 女 woman + 子 child · [明|míng] bright = 日 sun + 月 moon
One side gives the area of meaning, the other gives a rough sound. **Over 80% of characters are this type.**
[妈|mā] mother = 女 (woman) + 马 (mǎ, gives the sound) · [河|hé] river = 氵 (water) + 可 (kě)

blocks.text: That last row is the good news: Chinese characters are **not** blind memorization. Once you know a hundred or so basic components, new characters become guessable — the area of meaning from the radical, the rough sound from the other side.
The most common radicals

blocks.title: Stroke order rules
items: **Top to bottom**, **left to right**. These two rules alone cover most characters.
**Horizontal before vertical**: 十 is written — first, then ∣.
**Outside before inside**, closing stroke last: 国 is written 冂 → the inside → ㇐ closing the bottom.
**Middle before the sides**: 小 starts with the center stroke.
Stroke order isn't just etiquette — handwriting dictionaries and handwriting keyboards on phones use it to recognize the character you write.

blocks.title: Simplified vs traditional characters
items: This course uses **simplified characters** (简体字 jiǎntǐzì) throughout — the ones used in mainland China and Singapore.
Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau use **traditional characters** (繁體字 fántǐzì). Same language, different shapes: 汉 = 漢, 学 = 學, 说 = 說.
For beginners: pick one and master it. The second is far easier to learn later once the first is solid.

blocks.text: Every pattern used in the twelve units of this course, gathered in one place for a quick look before you speak. The unit column shows where each pattern is introduced.
Sentence frames

head: Pattern
What it does
Example
Unit
rows: A **is** B. ⚠️ Only for noun = noun, **never** with adjectives.
A is … . 很 is a required support word; it doesn't mean “very”.
Turns a statement into a yes/no question.
Choice question, same meaning as 吗.
不 = not (now, habits, will). 没 = didn't / hasn't happened (past) & 没有.
[我不去|Wǒ bú qù]。[我没去|Wǒ méi qù]。
Possession & description: A 的 B = A's B.
有 = there is / have. 在 = be located at. 是 = is.
[我有书|Wǒ yǒu shū]。[书在桌子上|Shū zài zhuōzi shang]。
Marks a **change / completed** action — not a past tense.
Have ever experienced, at least once in your life.

blocks.text: Question words
⚠️ Mandarin question words **do not move to the front of the sentence**. They stand exactly where the answer will stand. [你去哪儿|Nǐ qù nǎr]？ → [我去学校|Wǒ qù xuéxiào]。 Exactly the same order.

head: Question word
Meaning
Example
rows: [你什么时候来|Nǐ shénme shíhou lái]？
[你为什么不来|Nǐ wèishénme bù lái]？
how many / how much (large amounts, prices)

head: Word
Meaning
Example

[可以坐这儿吗|Kěyǐ zuò zhèr ma]？
[我要一杯茶|Wǒ yào yì bēi chá]。
[我喜欢中国菜|Wǒ xǐhuan Zhōngguó cài]。

blocks.text: Whenever a number meets a noun in Mandarin, a measure word must stand between them. English does something similar with some nouns (*two **pieces** of paper*, *three **cups** of tea*), but only some. Mandarin requires it for every noun — 三书 is as wrong as saying “three paper”.

head: Measure word
Used for
Example
rows: General — use it when you don't know the right one
Flat things: paper, tables, tickets, beds, photos
Family members (only when counting a household)
[五口人|wǔ kǒu rén] five people in the family
[两位老师|liǎng wèi lǎoshī] two teachers
[一杯茶|yì bēi chá] a cup of tea
[两瓶水|liǎng píng shuǐ] two bottles of water
[一碗面|yì wǎn miàn] a bowl of noodles
[一件衣服|yí jiàn yīfu] a piece of clothing
Long things: trousers, fish, roads, rivers, dogs
Most animals, one of a pair
[一双鞋|yì shuāng xié] a pair of shoes
[一家饭馆|yì jiā fànguǎn] a restaurant
Some (indefinite amount, never with a number other than 一)
[一点儿水|yìdiǎnr shuǐ] a little water

blocks.title: Three lifesavers
items: ⚠️ **两, not 二, before a measure word.** [两个|liǎng ge], [两本|liǎng běn], [两点|liǎng diǎn]. 二 is for counting, numbers, and digits inside larger numbers: [二十|èrshí], [十二|shí'èr].
If you truly forget the measure word, use **个**. It sounds a bit childish, but it's understood — far better than stopping mid-sentence.
Measure words are also required after 这 (this), 那 (that), and 哪 (which): [这本书|zhè běn shū], not 这书.

blocks.text: These are all the characters that appear again and again in the twelve units of this course. Master them and you can read most simple everyday sentences. They are listed in the order they appear in the course, not dictionary order — so you can use this list as a study schedule: ten characters a day, done in fifteen days.

If you reach this page after really working through all twelve units — not just skimming them — you are now around **HSK 2**: roughly 300 words, the full set of basic sentence frames, and the ability to get by in slow everyday conversation. That is far more than people imagine a “beginner level” to be.
Your next three steps, in order

items: **Grow your vocabulary to 600 before chasing new grammar.** At this point you get stuck not because you don't know the pattern, but because you don't know the word. Add ten words a day for two months.
**Start reading without pīnyīn.** Take Units 1 to 4 of this course, cover the pīnyīn with a strip of paper, and read them again. It will feel hard for the first five minutes and normal by day three.

**Find a real conversation partner.** Tones can't be fixed on your own through two hundred hours of self-study; they need someone who corrects you in the sixth second. This is where a teacher stops being a luxury.

blocks.title: If you'd like to continue with Linguo
items: **Private Mandarin classes** — one teacher, one student, on your schedule, online or in person. The fastest way to fix your tones.
**Semi-private classes** — two to four people, a lower fee, and partners to practice conversation with.
**HSK preparation classes** — if your goal is a scholarship, a job, or university in China.
All class information, schedules, and fees are at **linguo.id**.

blocks.text: One last line, from a saying Chinese people use for things that are long and hard: [千里之行|Qiān lǐ zhī xíng]，[始于足下|shǐ yú zú xià] — a journey of a thousand li begins with a single step beneath your feet. These twelve units are your first step. 加油！
